paras: The attempted lynching of Gaetano Gamardelli and Napoleon Ems took place at Rye, New York, on July 16, 1888, when about 300 armed Italian laborers marched on a justice's office and demanded two arrested men so that they might lynch them. A constable and armed citizens of Rye kept the crowd back and took the prisoners to White Plains prison, and the New York Tribune headlined the story "Saved From Being Lynched."

Large gangs of Italian laborers were then working on the roads and railroad near Harrison, West Chester and Rye, living in shanty camps along the line. According to the Tribune, rivalry and ill feeling between the gangs had led to repeated disturbances. On the evening of Sunday, July 8, Gamardelli, who kept a liquor store at Westchester, entered the Harrison camp threatening violence, and Louis Conventi and others disarmed him and drove him away.

Between 11 and 12 on the following Sunday night, the Tribune said, Gamardelli returned with Napoleon Emgalias Cabello, whom the paper also called Ems. Gamardelli was accused of shooting Lorenzo Veritto in the eye, and Ems of clubbing Angelo Gleiss with a shotgun butt and fracturing his skull, after each man failed to say where Conventi was. The Tribune added that Gamardelli fired at the sleeping Conventi and took $10 from him at pistol point before the two fled, while the wire version said only that they "shot several" of the Harrison Italians.

Roused at half-past four the next morning, Constable Samuel Graham of Rye followed the pair to Mamaroneck, boarded their departing train, handcuffed them and brought them to Justice Downing's office at Rye. When word of the arrest reached the camp, about 300 Italians armed with guns, revolvers and knives marched to the office and shouted for the prisoners' surrender "that they might lynch them." The Tribune described Ems taunting the crowd while Gamardelli fell to his knees and begged to be moved to safety.

Justice Henderson of Portchester sent for police reinforcements, but before they came some Rye citizens armed themselves with pistols and formed a bodyguard. Graham repeatedly charged the crowd to hold it off, and the prisoners were taken by wagon to White Plains prison "with the greatest difficulty," in the wire's words.

Gleiss was reported in a dangerous condition and Veritto's wound slight, and the two prisoners, who declined to answer the charge, were to be examined the next day. No report of that hearing, of any indictment or trial, or of action against members of the crowd was found.

The New York Tribune carried the fullest report on July 17 under the headlines "Saved From Being Lynched" and "Citizens of Rye Form a Body Guard," calling the crowd "would-be lynchers" and the prisoners "desperados." A shorter New York dispatch, which follows the Tribune's opening almost word for word, ran the same day in the Washington Critic and the next day in the Richmond Daily Times as "Riotous Italians." Its subhead spoke of an attempt to "Rescue a Disorderly Compatriot from Custody," although its own text said the crowd wanted the prisoners lynched.

In Dakota Territory the Jamestown Weekly Alert printed a condensed version on July 19 headed "Railroaders Riotous," naming no one and calling the two men "Murderers," though no report states that anyone had died. All of the coverage treated the affair as a feud among Italian work gangs, and none of it described anyone by race.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Gaetano Gamardelli and Napoleon Ems at Rye
bases: An armed crowd of about 300 marched on a justice's office demanding two prisoners so that it might lynch them, and was held off by a constable and armed citizens (A1, A3, A4).

No one was killed: a crowd of about 300 sought to lynch two men accused of shooting and clubbing camp residents, but officers and armed Rye citizens removed them to White Plains prison (A1, A3, A4). It was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The New York Tribune account (A1) is the only detailed report; the wire versions (A2, A3, A4) repeat its opening wording almost word for word and appear to be condensed from it or from the same New York source, so they do not count as independent reports.

info: Earlier quarrel on Sunday evening, July 8, 1888, when Gamardelli threatened men at the Harrison camp and was disarmed and driven away; not the date of the attempted lynching.
Shooting at the Italian laborers' camp at Harrison; the crowd gathered at Justice Downing's office in Rye; prisoners taken to White Plains prison.

The would-be lynching targets were the two prisoners, Gaetano Gamardelli (printed 'Gactano' in the Tribune), a liquor-store keeper at Westchester, and Napoleon Emgalias (or Emgolios) Cabello, called 'Ems' in the Tribune. Lorenzo Veritto and Angelo Gleiss were the men wounded in the shooting they were accused of.

Accused of shooting Lorenzo Veritto in the eye (Gamardelli), clubbing Angelo Gleiss with a shotgun butt and fracturing his skull (Ems), firing at the sleeping Louis Conventi and taking $10 from him at pistol point; the wire says the two 'shot several' of the Harrison Italians. Called 'robbery' by the Italian who roused the constable.
Italians from the Harrison camp, railroad and road laborers.
The prisoners were taken by wagon to White Plains prison; an examination or hearing was set for the next day. No report of the hearing, an indictment or a trial was found.
